title: Overflow and Scroll Behavior
subtopics: Visible, hidden, clipped, and scrollable overflow
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of overflow and scroll behavior.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on overflow and scroll behavior and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: Overflow and Scroll Behavior helps you build layouts that remain consistent as content, viewport width and component context change.

content_blocks.caption: Learning map for Module 5, from the opening concept to a practical checkpoint.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Visible, hidden, clipped, and scrollable overflow; Horizontal and vertical overflow; Overscroll behavior; Nested scrolling regions; Preventing undesirable scroll behavior. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

items: Visible, hidden, clipped, and scrollable overflow

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Overflow and Scroll Behavior
content_blocks.code: <button class="rounded-lg bg-slate-900 px-4 py-2 text-white transition-transform duration-200 hover:-translate-y-0.5 motion-reduce:transition-none motion-reduce:hover:translate-y-0">Explore</button>
content_blocks.expected_output: The button adds restrained hover feedback and removes the motion when reduced motion is requested.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to overflow and scroll behavior, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating overflow and scroll behavior. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to overflow and scroll behavior.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to overflow and scroll behavior.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: The button adds restrained hover feedback and removes the motion when reduced motion is requested.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying overflow and scroll behavior without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Overflow and Scroll Behavior is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
